name: data.police.uk public JSON API
geo_coverage: England & Wales (Home Office territorial forces plus British Transport Police)
caveats: Coordinates are snapped to a pre-built master list of anonymous map points - never the true location (see benchmark-police-uk-anonymisation-method)
The JSON API does not return LSOA codes; any area aggregation must go through the bulk CSV
Month granularity only - no day and no time of day anywhere in the public data
Category list is month-dependent, which is why /crime-categories takes a date parameter
Leaky-bucket rate limit: 15 requests/second, burst 30; no authentication
Endpoint paths for senior officers, neighbourhood events/priorities, outcomes-for-crime, stops-at-location and stops-no-location are INFERRED from an MCP client's tool names, not seen in fetched code
evidence: Endpoint list read from fetched working client code (Mta-adham/IngestEngine, src/clients/police_uk.py): /forces, /{force}/neighbourhoods, /{force}/{nh}/boundary, /locate-neighbourhood, /crime-categories, /crimes-street/{category}, /crimes-at-location, /crimes-no-location, /outcomes-at-location, /stops-street, /stops-force, /crime-last-updated, /crimes-street-dates. Rate-limit wording quoted from the ukpolice R package vignette; example calls reproduced from jdorfman/awesome-json-datasets and hrbrmstr/jwatr; a polygon call for date=2026-07 captured in kyky2347/pulse-london fixtures dated 2026-09-11. data.police.uk was egress-blocked from this session (CONNECT tunnel failed, 403); no official police.uk page was fetched.
notes: Crime object fields: id, persistent_id, category, month, context, location_type, location_subtype, location{latitude,longitude,street{id,name}}, outcome_status{category,date}. POST works as well as GET. Call-limit doc cited by two client libraries at https://data.police.uk/docs/api-call-limits/ (unfetched). This is the shape benchmark for our own /v1 API design (dossier section B).

name: police.uk bulk CSV downloads / monthly archive
geo_coverage: England & Wales (per-force directories inside each monthly archive)
time_start: 2010-12 historically; ~2023-06 in the live rolling window as of 2026
caveats: Retention: an ingestion project active in 2026 reports data.police.uk keeps only a rolling ~3-year window, earliest available June 2023 - if you do not archive it yourself the publisher will delete your history
Crime ID is reportedly blank for anti-social-behaviour rows and ASB has no outcome; the blank-Crime-ID rule is widely believed but was NOT confirmed in any fetched source
Longitude/Latitude are snapped and are blank where the nearest map point was over 20 km away
Location is always the string 'On or near <street>' - never a house number, by design
Context column is free text and almost always empty
evidence: 12-column street schema (Crime ID, Month, Reported by, Falls within, Longitude, Latitude, Location, LSOA code, LSOA name, Crime type, Last outcome category, Context) confirmed identically across five independent repositories; a sample row was read from AlistairLR112/EnglandCrimeAssociations (2012-08, Metropolitan Police, -0.508053, 50.809718, 'On or near Claigm...', E01031464, Arun 007F, Violent crime, Under investigation). Archive URL pattern reproduced from a working fetch script (SocialCatalystLab/ape-papers apep_0472 code/01_fetch_data.R); retention claim from djshaf/NightRunner. data.police.uk was egress-blocked from this session (CONNECT tunnel failed, 403); no official police.uk page was fetched.
notes: Archive URL pattern: https://data.police.uk/data/archive/{YYYY-MM}.zip, containing {force}/{YYYY-MM}-street.csv plus -outcomes.csv and -stop-and-search.csv. The CSV, not the API, is the real data product - it is the only route that carries LSOA codes. Dossier conclusion: ship a bulk file from day one.

name: police.uk location-anonymisation methodology (About page, #location-anonymisation)
time_start: 2012 (master map-point list built from Ordnance Survey data)
time_latest: current page as quoted by third parties
caveats: The published map-point count disagrees across three independent third-party projects (680,000 / ~750,000 / ~760,000) and none cites an official page reference - treat '~750,000' as folklore until the official page is re-read
The official page was NOT fetched this session; the rule is quoted at one remove from a data-journalism post that reproduces it and links the anchor
Snapping concentrates incidents on street centroids, car parks and station forecourts, producing phantom hotspots
No official average snap-point spacing is published; the only figure available is an empirical ~125 m upper bound from one 6-month Camden pull (1,384 distinct snap points over ~21.8 sq km)
ASB handling: ASB is snapped by the same process, but the blank-Crime-ID / no-outcome rule was not confirmed in a fetched source
evidence: Rule reproduced verbatim from egrommet/egrommet.github.io (post/data-police-location-issues), which quotes the official page and links the #location-anonymisation anchor: every crime's exact location is compared against a master list of anonymous map points, each sitting over a street centre / public place / commercial premise with a catchment of at least eight postal addresses or none at all; coordinates are replaced by the map point's, and zeroed out if the nearest map point is more than 20 km away; 'No other filtering or rules are applied'. Independently restated in two university GIS coursebooks (jo-wilkin/GEOG0030, jtvandijk/GEOG0030_20232024), which add the BNG-to-WGS84 conversion. data.police.uk was egress-blocked from this session (CONNECT tunnel failed, 403); no official police.uk page was fetched.
notes: Five design properties the dossier recommends copying: the point list is fixed and pre-computed (deterministic, no jitter leak); snapping is k-anonymity by construction rather than invertible random displacement; points are deliberately sited on non-homes; the k threshold (8 addresses) is published; and the fallback is deletion, not approximation - which is why crimes-no-location exists as a first-class endpoint. India cannot reproduce this: there is no open national address-point register to build a provable k>=8 snap list from.

name: police.uk crime categories (14) and outcomes model (9)
caveats: 14 buckets are coarse: 'Violence and sexual offences' merges a pub fight and a rape; 'Other theft' absorbs a large residual
The category list is month-dependent - historic 2012 rows carry the older label 'Violent crime'
Beyond the 9 published outcome categories the served data also contains 'Status update unavailable' and 'Court result unavailable'
Outcome categories merge distinguishable legal states into indistinguishable 'unresolved' (noted by Adam-Ansar/west-midlands-crime-analysis)
Anti-social behaviour has no outcome at all
evidence: Category slugs (anti-social-behaviour, bicycle-theft, burglary, criminal-damage-arson, drugs, other-theft, possession-of-weapons, public-order, robbery, shoplifting, theft-from-the-person, vehicle-crime, violence-and-sexual-offences, other-crime) reproduced from Janusz99bis/bigdata-crimes-airbnb-project and corroborated by the GEOG0030 coursebook section 'Coding of Crimes into 14 Categories'. Outcome distribution 2012-2016 read from BBC-Data-Unit/unsolved-crime: 'Investigation complete; no suspect identified' 9,424,687; 'Under investigation' 2,427,381; 'Unable to prosecute suspect' 1,649,291; 'Court result unavailable' 715,163; 'Offender given a caution' 611,237; 'Local resolution' 482,307. data.police.uk was egress-blocked from this session (CONNECT tunnel failed, 403); no official police.uk page was fetched.
notes: The modal outcome of a recorded crime in England & Wales is that nobody was identified, and police.uk shows that per crime on the map - the dossier calls this the single most credibility-building feature of the product. India's structural analogue is NCRB charge-sheeting and conviction rates. The date parameter on /crime-categories is the design detail India needs for the IPC-to-BNS transition.

name: police.uk neighbourhood policing team boundaries and locate-neighbourhood
geo_coverage: England & Wales (neighbourhood policing team areas within each force)
caveats: Boundaries are returned as a bare lat/lng vertex list, not GeoJSON - the caller has to assemble polygons
Neighbourhood team areas are an operational policing geography, not a statistical one, and do not align with LSOAs
Endpoint paths seen in fetched client code; no official documentation page was read
evidence: GET /{force}/{neighbourhood}/boundary and GET /locate-neighbourhood?q={lat},{lng} observed in fetched working client code (Mta-adham/IngestEngine, src/clients/police_uk.py); /{force}/neighbourhoods example call reproduced from jdorfman/awesome-json-datasets (https://data.police.uk/api/leicestershire/neighbourhoods). data.police.uk was egress-blocked from this session (CONNECT tunnel failed, 403); no official police.uk page was fetched.
notes: This is a distinct product surface from the crime map - 'who polices here' rather than 'what happened here' - and the dossier argues it is the one India can build best, because every Indian police station has a jurisdiction, a phone number and an SHO.

name: police.uk stop and search data
caveats: Records where a stop happened, which is a policing-activity geography, not a crime geography
Carries self-defined and officer-defined ethnicity, age range and gender - the fields that make disproportionality measurable, and the fields that must never enter a consumer safety product
Endpoint paths /stops-at-location and /stops-no-location are inferred from an MCP client's tool names, not seen in fetched code
evidence: /stops-street and /stops-force observed in fetched client code (Mta-adham/IngestEngine); field list (type, object of search, outcome, datetime, self-defined and officer-defined ethnicity, age range, gender) and the downstream retention policy read from djshaf/NightRunner, which deliberately drops gender, age range and ethnicity as 'sensitive personal data with no legitimate role in a safety score'. data.police.uk was egress-blocked from this session (CONNECT tunnel failed, 403); no official police.uk page was fetched.
notes: The dossier's rule for India: demographic breakdowns of police action belong in an accountability product, where they are the point, and must never appear in a neighbourhood safety product, where they become a caste/religion risk score for a locality.

name: Documented failure modes of police.uk (snap-point artefacts, false precision, small-number noise)
publisher: Various - local journalism, university coursebooks and downstream consumers, compiled by the benchmark-product agent
caveats: This entry is a synthesis of third-party criticism, not a dataset; no primary article URL was captured
The original Conor Gogarty / Bristol Live article was not located this session - it is Seed Lead 7
The peer-reviewed literature on crime maps and house prices, and the 2011-era ICO/Home Office granularity debate, were not reachable (arxiv.org and gov.uk blocked) - Seed Leads 5 and 6
evidence: Via egrommet/egrommet.github.io: journalist Conor Gogarty found 41 shoplifting offences mapped to a location with no nearby shops; police confirmed the markers are snap points and a Home Office spokesperson attributed the inaccuracies to 'inconsistent geocoding policies'. A fetched commercial property-research tool (soreavis/property-deep-dive) describes the UK as 'Best-in-Class Parcel-Level Data' with 'address-level crime data', which is flatly wrong. A fetched working product spec (Demonstrandum/floot) states the counter-rule - 'Resolution is street segment, not address. Never present one snap point as crime at this address' - and applies a 400 m buffer plus empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the borough mean, reporting a London percentile rather than an absolute rate. maczokni/crime_mapping notes LSOAs 'may not bear much resemblance to what residents might think of as their neighbourhood'.
notes: Six failure modes to design against: (a) phantom hotspots from snapping plus inconsistent force geocoding; (b) false precision downstream - a commercial consumer relabels street segments as addresses and sells them to a landlord; (c) small-number noise - street-level counts are often below 20 incidents a year; (d) denominator errors - footfall-driven acquisitive crime must be normalised by workday population, residential crime by resident population and burglary by household count, or Old Street looks dangerous purely because of pedestrian volume; (e) jurisdictional contamination - British Transport Police records must be excluded or every flat near a station looks terrible (India's analogue is the GRP); (f) category coarseness.

name: Lower Layer Super Output Area (LSOA) - the small-area geography police.uk tags crimes with
caveats: Every quantitative claim about LSOAs in the dossier is UNVERIFIED: ons.gov.uk was egress-blocked, so the ~1,500 target population, the minimum 1,000 residents / 400 households design constraint, and the ~34,700 (2011) / ~35,700 (2021) counts could not be checked
No ONS URL was captured - the entry carries no link deliberately, rather than a guessed one
The catalogue enum has no small-area statistical level; LSOA is recorded here as `ward`, which is the nearest available value and is coarser than the real unit
LSOAs 'may not bear much resemblance to what residents might think of as their neighbourhood'
evidence: Only the code and name format was actually seen, inside fetched police.uk CSV samples: LSOA code E01031464, LSOA name 'Arun 007F'. The design constraints and LSOA counts are reproduced from the project brief and could not be confirmed against ons.gov.uk, which was egress-blocked.
notes: The three properties that make LSOA work and that India must reproduce or abandon: stable codes with a published change history; a population denominator published at the same geography and refreshed annually; open boundary polygons. India has no unit that is simultaneously LSOA-sized, publicly boundaried and attached to a fresh denominator - the revenue village is the closest by population but rural-only with patchy boundaries, the census enumeration block is the right size but is not published as a geography, and the police station is the unit the data is actually recorded in. Geography roadmap: district now, police station when the boundaries are won, never point.

name: Crime Survey for England and Wales (CSEW)
publisher: Office for National Statistics; fieldwork by Verian (formerly Kantar Public); microdata curated by the UK Data Service
time_start: 1982 (as the British Crime Survey); continuous interviewing from April 2001
caveats: Excludes the non-household population (~1.7% of England & Wales: care homes, prisons, homeless)
Excludes homicide and victimless crimes such as drug possession
Sample size (~31,000 adults 16+, ~1,500 children 10-15 per year) cannot support rare high-harm crimes
Historically undercounted repeat victimisation such as domestic violence through capping
No ONS or UK Data Service URL was captured - ons.gov.uk was egress-blocked
Formats are inferred (ONS publishes headline tables as spreadsheets); the dossier does not state them
evidence: Design facts reproduced in the dossier from the project brief and fetched secondary material: established 1982 as the British Crime Survey, four-yearly at first, continuous from April 2001; ~31,000 adults plus ~1,500 children 10-15 a year; reported by financial year with headline measures updated quarterly on a rolling 12-month basis; by 1998 police received reports for fewer than half of all offences that occurred. No ONS page was fetched.
how_to_obtain: Headline tables are published openly by ONS. Respondent-level microdata is login-gated: register with the UK Data Service, accept the End User Licence and download the study; Special Licence/Secure Lab access is needed for the more detailed files.
notes: The reason this entry is priority 5 in a benchmark domain: England & Wales pair a near-complete police-recorded series with a survey that corrects it at the margin, whereas India will pair a demonstrably incomplete police-recorded series with a survey. A district with low recorded crime against women may have low crime or a police station that refuses to register FIRs, and only survey prevalence separates the two. India's analogues are NFHS (spousal-violence and help-seeking modules at district level) and SPIR - both belong to other agents' domains. The agent's recommendation is that the map must not ship without one wired in.

name: FBI Crime Data Explorer (CDE) / National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS)
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, CJIS - Uniform Crime Reporting Program
geo_coverage: United States (agency-level submissions aggregated to state and national)
time_start: 1988 (NIBRS approved at a national UCR conference in March 1988); sole FBI collection standard from 1 January 2021
time_latest: Q4 2023 coverage figures cited (15,199 agencies, 82% of population)
taxonomy: custom (NIBRS Group A: 52 offences in 23 categories; Group B: 10 arrest-only offences)
caveats: CDE does not publish incident coordinates - US point-level data comes from cities, not the FBI; the catalogue enum has no 'agency' level so the submitting agency's jurisdiction is recorded here as police-district

The mid-series transition broke the national trend line for roughly three years: 11,794 agencies and 69% population coverage on 1 Jan 2022; by Q2 2023, with 13,363 agencies, the FBI stated it was 'unable to make confident statements about national crime trends'; 15,199 agencies and 82% coverage by Q4 2023
Coverage is voluntary agency submission, so absence is non-response, not absence of crime
No URL captured: api.usa.gov was egress-blocked this session and the dossier records no CDE endpoint
evidence: NIBRS structure described in the dossier from fetched secondary sources: no Hierarchy Rule (all offences in a multi-offence incident are recorded, unlike Summary UCR's most-serious-only), three offence classes (Crimes Against Persons, Property and Society), and seven linked segments per incident - offence (with location type, weapons, completion status), victim, offender, property, arrestee, plus zero-reporting. Agency-count and coverage figures as listed in the caveats. No FBI page was fetched.
how_to_obtain: Free api.data.gov key for the CDE API; bulk CSV extracts are also published. No endpoint URL was captured this session - re-verify in Phase 2.
notes: The abolition of the Hierarchy Rule is precisely the NCRB principal-offence-rule problem, and NIBRS is the proof both that abolishing it is possible and what it costs. India is running the same experiment now with the IPC-to-BNS transition (in force 1 July 2024): expect 2-4 years in which no honest year-on-year comparison spans the break, and mark it on every chart.

name: Chicago Crimes, 2001-Present
publisher: Chicago Police Department / City of Chicago Data Portal (Socrata)
caveats: US cities publish incident records with coordinates and block-truncated addresses (e.g. '0XX N STATE ST') with no snap-point anonymisation layer; there is no national US anonymisation standard, each city invents one

Block-level publication plus daily cadence lets a determined observer identify the household, catastrophically so for domestic violence and sexual offences - US cities suppress or generalise those categories inconsistently
Endpoint cited from third-party pipelines; the portal itself was blocked this session
evidence: Dataset identifier and endpoint reproduced in the dossier from multiple independent ingestion pipelines. data.cityofchicago.org was egress-blocked this session and no city portal was fetched directly.
notes: Bulk CSV: https://data.cityofchicago.org/api/views/ijzp-q8t2/rows.csv

publisher: New York City Police Department / NYC Open Data (Socrata)
caveats: US cities publish incident records with coordinates and block-truncated addresses (e.g. '0XX N STATE ST') with no snap-point anonymisation layer; there is no national US anonymisation standard, each city invents one
The same series arrives from two endpoints with two different lags - Historic (~annual) and Year-To-Date (~quarterly) - and consumers must query and merge both
Endpoints cited from third-party pipelines; the portal itself was not fetched
evidence: Dataset identifier and endpoint reproduced in the dossier from multiple independent ingestion pipelines. data.cityofchicago.org was egress-blocked this session and no city portal was fetched directly.

Bulk CSV: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/api/views/qgea-i56i/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD. The historic/YTD split is the pattern we will face with Indian state portals - design ingestion for it.

publisher: Denver Police Department / Denver Open Data (ArcGIS)
caveats: US cities publish incident records with coordinates and block-truncated addresses (e.g. '0XX N STATE ST') with no snap-point anonymisation layer; there is no national US anonymisation standard, each city invents one
Refreshed on weekdays only, per the dossier's table - recorded here as daily
Endpoint cited, not fetched

name: Crime Open Database (CODE)
caveats: Verification is VERIFIED_LANDING carried over from the dossier: the OSF landing page was reached, the data files themselves were not opened
An academic harmonisation layer, so it inherits every source city's coverage gaps and lags
evidence: OSF landing page https://osf.io/zyaqn/ reached; project described as 'a service that makes it convenient to use crime data from multiple US cities in research on crime', free to use with acknowledgement. The repository's code/02_load_crime_data.R was read and shows per-city download plus recoding into a common offence scheme (e.g. 'ARSON' ~ '200 Arson'). Data files not opened.
notes: The design precedent for India's hardest problem - many publishers, incompatible taxonomies, one comparable output. What to copy: a published crosswalk table, a versioned harmonised category scheme, and honest per-city coverage notes. This is our IPC/BNS-to-common-category mapping problem, already solved once for another country.

name: SpotCrime
caveats: Address-level publication plus 2026 'address safety scores' and trends - the dossier names this explicitly as the line a public-interest Indian product must not cross
Sources are a mix of direct law-enforcement feeds (CAD, blotters), open portals, FOIA responses and verified news, so coverage is a feed-availability map, not a crime map
500M+ records is a vendor claim, unaudited
evidence: From a fetched 2026 competitive audit (GojoCookz/Cyclopalypse, docs/competitive-audit-2026.md); the vendor's own site was not fetched.
how_to_obtain: The consumer map at spotcrime.com is free and ad-supported; programmatic access requires an API subscription - Developer $199/month, Pro $599/month, Enterprise by negotiation.
notes: Anti-pattern reference value is high (the dossier rates it priority 5 as an anti-pattern, 1 as a data source).

name: LexisNexis Community Crime Map (formerly RAIDS Online)
caveats: Published at block level (the catalogue enum has no 'block' value; recorded here as address)
Suffered a 2024 breach affecting 364,000+ people, disclosed in 2025 - centralising agency data is itself a liability
Coverage is a function of which agencies contract, not of where crime happens
evidence: From a fetched 2026 competitive audit (GojoCookz/Cyclopalypse, docs/competitive-audit-2026.md); the vendor's own site was not fetched. Data described as direct agency RMS/CAD feeds, 'cleaned, geocoded and redacted'.
how_to_obtain: The public map is free to browse but there is no public bulk export; programmatic use means scraping the map tiles/endpoints or being a contracting agency (B2G). Check the terms of use before any scrape.
notes: Read as a governance warning, not as a source.

name: CrimeMapping.com
caveats: Opt-in agencies only, so the coverage map is a participation map: a blank area means 'no contract', not 'no crime' - the single most important misreading to design against
Published at 'block-level privacy'; the catalogue enum has no 'block' value, recorded here as address
evidence: From a fetched 2026 competitive audit (GojoCookz/Cyclopalypse, docs/competitive-audit-2026.md); the vendor's own site was not fetched.
how_to_obtain: Public map is free to browse; no bulk export. Data arrives through the vendor's B2G SaaS contract with each agency; programmatic use means scraping under the site's terms.
notes: Named in the brief as a benchmark product. Also referenced by a peer project's source-discovery skill (BSteffaniak/crime-map, Seed Lead 13).

name: CityProtect
caveats: Publishes calls for service as well as verified offences - a distinct and much noisier product; a call is a report of a suspicion, not a crime
Retention is only 180 days to 1 year, so it cannot support a trend series
Opt-in coverage; no URL was recorded in the dossier
evidence: From a fetched 2026 competitive audit (GojoCookz/Cyclopalypse, docs/competitive-audit-2026.md); the vendor's own site was not fetched.
how_to_obtain: Public map only; no bulk export and no URL captured in the dossier. Programmatic use means scraping the public map under its terms, or an agency contract.
notes: The calls-for-service distinction is a hard exclusion in the dossier's product rules: ERSS-112 call volumes must never be presented as crime, because they measure calling, and Indian 112 usage varies by an order of magnitude between states.

name: Citizen (formerly Vigilante)
caveats: Built from unencrypted public-safety radio plus AI transcription, human analysts and user video - unverified by construction
Roughly 300-400 incidents surfaced daily out of NYC's ~10,000 calls, so the feed is a heavy editorial filter presented as a live truth
Launched as 'Vigilante' in 2016 and pulled from the App Store within 48 hours for encouraging mob justice
In the 2021 Palisades Fire it posted a photo of an innocent man as the suspected arsonist with a $30,000 bounty; he was questioned and exonerated
evidence: From a fetched 2026 competitive audit (GojoCookz/Cyclopalypse, docs/competitive-audit-2026.md); the vendor's own site was not fetched. Corroborated by the Citizen Wikipedia article, which was fetched.
how_to_obtain: Consumer mobile app, freemium at $5.99-$19.99/month. No public API or export is recorded in the dossier.
notes: The clearest documented harm in the commercial tier, and the reason the dossier forbids real-time community incident reporting in v1.

name: CrimeGrade.org
caveats: Grades a block by model output where no data exists - FBI UCR/NIBRS plus local sources plus ML gap-filling across 180+ variables. The dossier's verdict: 'fabrication with a confidence interval'
Block-level A-F grades are recorded here as address granularity because the enum has no block level; the underlying data is agency-level
Free to consumers but licensed B2B to insurers and real estate, which is the pipeline where a crime map becomes a price
evidence: From a fetched 2026 competitive audit (GojoCookz/Cyclopalypse, docs/competitive-audit-2026.md); the vendor's own site was not fetched.
how_to_obtain: Public site is free to browse; no export. B2B licensing is by commercial agreement. Any programmatic use would be scraping under the site's terms.
notes: Cited in the dossier as the strongest argument for the rule 'rank, do not score' - percentiles within a state instead of grades.

name: Property-risk crime indexes: NeighborhoodScout (CoreLogic), AreaVibes, Niche, Verisk CAP Index
caveats: FBI-derived indexes are resold as neighbourhood and even address-specific scores - Verisk CAP Index runs 0-2000 at address level
AreaVibes lags a year or more; Niche is 37.5% resident survey, i.e. perception mixed into a crime number
Sold into real-estate lead generation and insurance underwriting - the point at which a crime map stops being information and becomes a price
No URLs were recorded in the dossier for any of the four
evidence: From a fetched 2026 competitive audit (GojoCookz/Cyclopalypse, docs/competitive-audit-2026.md); the vendor's own site was not fetched.
how_to_obtain: Commercial licences only; no open export. Recorded as an anti-pattern reference, not as an ingestion candidate.
notes: Grouped as one entry because the dossier describes them in a single table row with no individual URLs.

name: SAPS quarterly crime statistics (police-station level)
time_start: 1994-ish for the station series; 2020-01 in the clean reconstruction
taxonomy: custom (17 community-reported serious crime categories plus detected crimes)
caveats: The machine-readable numbers sit in HIDDEN Excel worksheets - the publisher ships a presentation artefact with the dataset buried inside it (a separate tool, afrith/unhide-xlsx, exists to unhide them). This is the NCRB PDF problem in another country

Station renaming and reorganisation is continuous: nine Eastern Cape stations renamed (Cradock to Nxuba, Grahamstown to Makhanda), fourteen name spellings standardised, two new stations (Phaudi, Majola) reallocated to parent districts - a crosswalk table is a first-class deliverable, not a cleanup step
Precinct polygons contain slivers and overlaps and needed PostGIS ST_CoverageClean
No point data whatsoever - aggregation to the precinct IS the anonymisation
Occurrence versus registration semantics are not stated by the publisher, hence jurisdiction-aggregate
www.saps.gov.za was egress-blocked this session; the landing URL is cited, not fetched
evidence: Structure described in the dossier from a working reconstruction (afrith/crime-stats): quarterly Excel workbooks at precinct level across 17 community-reported serious crime categories plus detected crimes (drug-related, driving under the influence, illegal firearms), culpable homicide, public violence and other offences. Older releases at https://www.saps.gov.za/services/older_crimestats.php. No SAPS page was fetched.
notes: The dossier's central recommendation: South Africa, not the UK, is the model India should copy. The police station is India's real administrative atom, its jurisdictions exist on paper, and per-station per-month per-head FIR counts are a record the police already keep. SAPS needs no anonymisation methodology at all because it never publishes a location. The station-level release created an ecosystem - GBV dashboards, academic theses, GeoParquet/PMTiles pipelines (ChelseaH93/sa-gbv-data) and Kaggle mirrors (slwessels/crime-statistics-for-south-africa).

name: Incidencia delictiva municipal (IDM) - SESNSP open data
publisher: Secretariado Ejecutivo del Sistema Nacional de Seguridad Publica (SESNSP), Mexico
time_latest: December 2025 data cut, June 2026 publication edition
lag: 1-3 months intended (published around the 20th for the prior month); months in practice
taxonomy: custom 4-level: bien juridico afectado (7) - tipo de delito (40) - subtipo (55) - modalidad (59)
caveats: Wide format: one row per year x municipality x taxonomy with 12 monthly columns - not a tidy series
The taxonomy grid grows over time (189,238 rows/year in 2015-16 to 243,628 in 2024-25) as municipalities and categories are added; never assume a constant Cartesian grid
Each monthly cut retroactively revises figures across the ENTIRE 2015-present history - snapshot every vintage and never overwrite
Dual-date filenames (dic25_corte_jun26) encode the data cutoff and the publication edition; these are two different dates and both must be modelled - an age badge needs the cutoff, not the edition
Encoding alternates between Latin-1 and UTF-8 between vintages
Cifra negra: the counts are delito denunciado y registrado, not crime that occurred; ENVIPE is the survey counterpart
datos.gob.mx serves an incomplete TLS certificate chain - bundle the Let's Encrypt intermediates
evidence: Access matrix verified on 2026-08-13 by an active ingestion project (jballesterosc/observatorio-delictivo-mx) whose code and notes the dossier fetched: the official gob.mx page is behind a JS anti-bot challenge and links to OneDrive with non-durable tokens; the CKAN package_show endpoint has returned 403 since 2026-08-13 (it worked on 2026-07-09); the repodatos.atdt.gob.mx mirror returns 200. Latest verified file IDM_NM_dic25.csv: 361 MB, 2,562,994 rows x 21 columns, Latin-1. SESNSP hosts were not fetched by this agent.
how_to_obtain: Do not use the official page - it is JS-challenged and its OneDrive links expire. Fetch the direct mirror https://repodatos.atdt.gob.mx/api_update/sesnsp/incidencia_delictiva/IDM_NM_{mmm}{yy}.csv with a Spanish three-letter month plus two-digit year (e.g. IDM_NM_dic25.csv), decoding Latin-1 with a UTF-8 fallback and bundling the Let's Encrypt intermediate certificates. Re-check the CKAN API periodically in case the 403 lifts.
notes: The cadence model for India, and a worked example of the failure to design against: a national monthly municipal series that is one CSV, published behind an increasingly hostile front door. Its three-date discipline (data cutoff, publication edition, vintage) is copied directly into the dossier's proposed crime-count record.

name: Fogo Cruzado - geocoded gun-violence occurrences API (v2)
geo_coverage: Rio de Janeiro, Greater Recife and expanding Brazilian metros
caveats: Crowdsourced reports plus verification: no denominator, no completeness guarantee, and a reporting bias toward areas with engaged reporters
Can only honestly be presented as 'reports we received', never as 'shootings that happened' - and that framing must be in the UI, not in a disclaimer
Requires registration for credentials; paginated
evidence: API v2 shape corroborated in three independent production pipelines including the Rio city government's own data platform (prefeitura-rio/pipelines_rj_civitas): POST /api/v2/auth/login returns a bearer token, GET /api/v2/states lists states and GET /api/v2/occurrences?page={n} returns per-occurrence records with municipality and geocode, aggregable by municipio. The API itself was not called by this agent.
how_to_obtain: Register at Fogo Cruzado for credentials, POST them to https://api-service.fogocruzado.org.br/api/v2/auth/login for a bearer token, then page through /api/v2/occurrences with an Authorization: Bearer header.
notes: The clearest working proof that a non-state actor can build a geocoded incident dataset the state itself then consumes - and simultaneously the clearest demonstration of why a crowdsourced feed cannot carry a rate. Directly relevant to any Safecity-style community reporting in India.

name: SSP-SP crime statistics and transparency portal (and the Brazilian state-secretariat pattern)
publisher: Secretaria de Seguranca Publica do Estado de Sao Paulo
geo_coverage: Sao Paulo state (and the template for all 26 Brazilian states plus the DF)
time_start: ~2016 for boletim de ocorrencia (BO) level records for the capital
caveats: Mixed unit of record: BO-level records for the capital, monthly aggregates elsewhere - the same endpoint family serves two different products
Every state secretariat publishes differently, behind its own paginated search form filtered by month or locality; there is no national endpoint
Occurrence versus registration semantics are not stated by the publisher
The transparency portal URL recorded in the dossier is plain HTTP
evidence: Described in the dossier from the R package brcrimR, which exists precisely because 'muitas Secretarias de Seguranca disponibilizam as informacoes filtradas por mes ou localidade' and whose stated purpose is 'iterar por essas paginas'. Neither SSP-SP host was fetched this session.
how_to_obtain: Scrape the paginated consultation forms per state, month and locality - brcrimR is an existing reference implementation. Expect one scraper per state plus a harmonisation layer; there is no bulk national download.
notes: The closest structural analogue to India that exists: a federal country where public security is a state subject, every state publishes differently, a few publish at incident level and most publish monthly aggregates behind a search form, and the only way to a national picture is per-state scraping plus harmonisation. Whatever Brazil had to build, India will have to build.
